clinicalPearls: Mesenteric cysts are rare intra-abdominal cysts arising within the mesentery, most commonly in the small bowel mesentery and particularly the ileum.

The de Perrot classification groups them by origin into lymphatic, mesothelial, enteric, urogenital, dermoid, and non-pancreatic pseudocyst types, with lymphatic (lymphangiomatous) lesions predominating.
Many are asymptomatic incidental findings; symptomatic lesions cause abdominal distension, vague pain, or a palpable mass.
The classic Tillaux sign is a mass that moves freely in a plane perpendicular to the axis of the mesentery but is restricted along it.
Complications include torsion, intracystic haemorrhage, infection, rupture, and bowel obstruction, any of which can produce an acute abdomen.
Ultrasound and CT typically show a thin-walled, well-defined, fluid-filled lesion; internal septation or chylous fluid suggests a lymphatic origin.
Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice and may require resection of intimately adherent bowel to ensure clearance.
Chylous ascites can accompany or follow lymphatic cysts and complicate surgical management.
reference.pathophysiology: Mesenteric cysts are benign lesions most often thought to result from proliferation of ectopic or maldeveloped lymphatic tissue that fails to establish communication with the normal lymphatic system, leading to progressive accumulation of lymph or chyle. Other histogenetic origins account for the mesothelial, enteric, and urogenital variants, reflecting entrapped embryonic tissues within the mesenteric leaves. The cyst enlarges as fluid accumulates, exerting mass effect on adjacent bowel and mesenteric vessels; because the lesion lies between the mesenteric leaves it can twist on its pedicle, bleed, become infected, or rupture. The lining varies with origin — endothelial in lymphatic cysts and mesothelial in mesothelial cysts — a distinction confirmed histologically and with immunohistochemistry.
additionalInvestigations: abdominal ultrasound to characterise the cyst and its septa
contrast-enhanced CT to define anatomy and vascular relationships
MRI for soft-tissue characterisation and surgical planning
analysis of aspirated fluid for chyle versus serous content
histopathology with endothelial and mesothelial immunohistochemical markers
redFlags: acute abdomen from torsion, intracystic haemorrhage, or rupture
rapid enlargement or systemic signs suggesting infection
solid or thickened components raising concern for cystic mesothelioma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent after complete excision, with cure and low recurrence. Incomplete removal of lymphatic lesions may be followed by recurrence.
pitfalls: misinterpreting a large cyst as free ascites on imaging
confusing the lesion with an ovarian cyst in female patients
incomplete excision of a lymphatic cyst leading to recurrence
underestimating the need for adjacent bowel resection when the cyst is inseparable from the mesenteric vessels
overlooking postoperative chylous leak after excision of a lymphatic cyst
management: Complete surgical excision as the definitive treatment, by laparoscopy or laparotomy, with enucleation where possible
Segmental bowel resection when the cyst is inseparable from adjacent bowel or its blood supply
Urgent surgery for acute complications such as torsion, intracystic haemorrhage, infection, rupture or bowel obstruction
Histopathological confirmation with immunohistochemistry to define origin and exclude malignancy
Marsupialisation or sclerotherapy only when complete excision is not feasible, accepting a higher recurrence risk
Follow-up for recurrence, particularly after incomplete removal of lymphatic lesions
